analysis.one_liner: Prohibits the largest digital ad companies from owning the ad auction and the brokers on both sides of it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to bar digital advertising giants like Google from owning both the ad auction and the brokers on each side of it was referred to the Judiciary Committee in May 2022 and died there with no hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a structural conflict in digital advertising: companies with more than $20 billion in annual digital ad revenue — Google is the example the official summary names — would be barred from owning more than one link in the ad-trading chain, such as owning the marketplace where ad space is auctioned while also running the software that sellers use to list space or the software that buyers use to bid [S2]. Companies with more than $5 billion in ad revenue acting as brokers would have a legal duty to act in their customers' best interest and get the best available price, with detailed transparency rules about bids, routing, and fees [S2] [S3]. Violations could be enforced by the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and private lawsuits [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that buy ads — including small businesses — and websites and publishers that sell ad space, who currently pay layers of fees to intermediaries often owned by the same dominant firm on both sides of the trade. Consumers benefit indirectly when advertising intermediation is cheaper and less conflicted, which supports a wider range of publishers, including news outlets. Smaller ad-tech firms also stand to gain once the dominant firms must divest overlapping businesses.

how_it_helps.text: Companies with over $20 billion in annual digital advertising revenue may not own more than one type of service in the digital advertising marketplace — for example, a company such as Google may not own a digital advertising exchange and also provide software that helps publishers sell ad space [S2].

Companies with over $5 billion in ad revenue that broker ad buys or sales must act in the best interest of their brokerage customers and seek the most favorable terms reasonably available for each customer's order [S2] [S3].

Brokerages above the $5 billion threshold must, on customer request, provide information verifying compliance — including all bids, winning prices, routing practices, and any compensation paid or received — and must publicly report their routing practices quarterly [S3].

Enforcement is available through the Department of Justice, state attorneys general, and a private right of action with damages of at least $1,000,000 per month of violation for harmed brokerage customers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The handful of dominant digital advertising companies — chiefly Google, and any other firm over the $20 billion threshold such as Meta or Amazon — which would have had one year after enactment to divest overlapping ad-exchange, buy-side, or sell-side businesses, with the Attorney General reviewing and approving required divestitures [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Forcing large firms to divest businesses within one year, with divestitures subject to Attorney General approval, could disrupt ad-auction technology and intermediate networks that many small publishers and advertisers currently rely on, at least during a transition [S3].

The compliance regime is demanding: firms over $5 billion face recordkeeping, time-synchronization to within 2 milliseconds of the NIST atomic clock, annual certification to the Attorney General, and detailed quarterly public routing reports — costs that critics said could raise the price of ad services [S3].

The bill addresses only the structure of ad trading; it does not cap ad prices directly, so whether savings reach advertisers and publishers depends on competition actually emerging after divestitures [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is significant and well documented in the bill's structure: it eliminates a specific, identifiable conflict of interest — one company operating the auction and the tools on both sides of it — and backs it with real enforcement teeth. The costs are transition and compliance burdens on a handful of firms, not on the public, though poorly managed divestitures could cause short-term disruption for the small publishers and advertisers the bill is meant to help. On balance the design is targeted rather than sweeping, which limits both its upside and its downside risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which took no further action, so it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 19, 2022, by Senator Mike Lee along with Senators Klobuchar, Cruz, and Blumenthal, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S3] [S5].
It ended the 117th Congress with a total of six cosponsors — 2 of 48 Senate Democrats and 4 of 50 Senate Republicans — and no action after the committee referral [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant digital advertising companies, above all Google, whose integrated ad-exchange and brokerage businesses were the bill's direct target, remain intact because the bill never received a hearing or vote. Advertisers and publishers continue paying the existing layers of intermediary fees.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Amy Klobuchar, Ted Cruz, and Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senators, original cosponsors (D-MN, R-TX, D-CT)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Google and the large digital advertising platforms
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed structural separation bills in the digital advertising and app-store space, arguing they would harm small publishers and raise costs.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split across parties — 2 of 48 Senate Democrats and 4 of 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored — and the bill was introduced jointly by two Republicans and two Democrats; no vote ever occurred to show how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: Dominant digital advertising companies (Google, and any firm above $20B in ad revenue, such as Meta or Amazon)
industries.note: They would have had one year to divest overlapping ad-exchange, buy-side, or sell-side businesses and face best-interest, transparency, and private-suit obligations. These firms profit from controlling multiple layers of the ad auction, which is exactly the conflict the bill was written to eliminate.

industries.industry: Ad brokers and exchanges above $5 billion in ad revenue
industries.note: They could keep operating but under a fiduciary-style best-interest and best-execution duty, detailed disclosure of bids, routing and fees, and annual certification — real regulation, not a prohibition on their business.
Structural separation of the dominant firms would open the ad-exchange and brokerage layers to competition from independents that cannot currently compete against a vertically integrated rival.
Best-execution duties and full visibility into bids, routing, and compensation would let them verify they are not paying hidden intermediary fees.

Sell-side transparency rules and an end to one company owning both the auction and the seller's tooling would strengthen publishers' ability to sell their ad inventory at competitive prices, which supports ad-funded content consumers use for free.
